video_title: Lawfare Daily: FCC’s Bad Labs Rulemaking with FCC’s Andy Hendrickson and Alice Jou
gist: FCC Office of Engineering and Technology officials Andy Hendrickson and Alice Jou explain how US RF-device testing migrated to China (US share of applications by testing-firm location fell from ~31% in 2007 to under 4% in 2025 while China rose from ~15% to ~82%), detail the Derrycom case (a Chinese-owned certification body posing as Minnesota-based that became the #4 TCB within 18 months), and lay out the 'bad labs' / equipment authorization integrity agenda culminating in a proposal to stop recognizing labs in non-reciprocal economies from December 1, 2028.

insights.claim: FCC equipment authorization data show the US share of applications by testing-firm location fell from about 31% in 2007 to below 4% in 2025, while the share tied to testing firms in China rose from about 15% to roughly 82%.
insights.speaker: Andy Hendrickson (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: US device certification has a strategic single-country dependency on China that regulators now intend to unwind.
insights.quote: In 2007, the United States accounted for about 31% of applications by testing firm location. And by 2025, it was below 4%.

insights.claim: The migration of device testing to China was driven by manufacturing relocation plus an FCC policy shift that prioritized accreditation/technical competence over reciprocity, letting foreign labs serve the US market while US labs lacked equal access abroad.
insights.speaker: Andy Hendrickson (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Regulatory design, not just labor cost, created the dependency, so regulatory reversal can partially undo it.
insights.quote: access became a one-way street in some places

insights.claim: The FCC names China, Switzerland and India as examples of non-reciprocal economies that do not accept US test lab results even though the US accepts theirs.
insights.speaker: Alice Jou (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Labs in these jurisdictions are the ones exposed to the proposed derecognition.
insights.quote: That is one way that our industry has gotten gutted over the last 20 years.

insights.claim: The FCC system currently recognizes about 600 test labs and about 40 telecommunications certification bodies (TCBs), and a small FCC lab team in Columbia, Maryland oversees tens of thousands of applications annually.
insights.speaker: Alice Jou / Andy Hendrickson (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: The program's scale relies almost entirely on private gatekeepers, so their integrity is the system's weak point.

insights.claim: Derrycom, a certification body registered at a small Minnesota address and approved in October 2024, became the #4 of 40 FCC certification bodies within 18 months, certifying almost 12,000 applications, and was the #2 body in Canada's market.
insights.speaker: Alice Jou (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: A front entity can capture large certification share quickly before regulators notice.
insights.quote: in less than 18 months, it had certified almost 12,000 applications by volume

insights.claim: The FCC investigation found Derrycom was 99% owned by a Chinese citizen, five of its six employees and four contract technical reviewers were in Shenzhen/China, and the listed US technical reviewer swore he never did any work for it.
insights.speaker: Alice Jou (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Penalty-of-perjury attestations are only meaningful when signers are reachable by US law.

insights.claim: Derrycom was suspended by its accreditor in May and cited by the FCC the following month for false statements about its location and for certifying devices and frequency bands outside its accreditation scope.
insights.speaker: Alice Jou (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: The FCC is now actively enforcing against certification bodies and signals more investigations.
insights.quote: The takeaway there is really just don't lie to the FCC.

insights.claim: The FCC expects to find more problem labs as it examines its data more closely and builds out a new cohort of attorneys drawn from big law, DOJ, and Commerce BIS/Office of ICTS.
insights.speaker: Alice Jou (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Expect further enforcement actions against test labs and TCBs, increasing compliance risk for China-based testing.
insights.quote: We think we're going to find more as we look more closely at our data

insights.claim: The FCC frames its equipment authorization integrity proceeding as three steps: a 2025 action barring labs/TCBs/accreditors owned or controlled by prohibited entities, an April 2026 action fast-tracking devices tested in trusted (US or reciprocal) labs, and a pending vote to stop recognizing labs in non-reciprocal economies.
insights.speaker: Andy Hendrickson (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Policy is moving from case-by-case policing to a structural jurisdiction-based rule.

insights.claim: The FCC proposes to stop recognizing test labs, certification bodies and accreditation bodies in non-reciprocal economies, with a proposed cutoff date of December 1, 2028, with the vote scheduled for late October.
insights.speaker: Alice Jou (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Device makers testing in China have roughly two years to shift testing to US or reciprocal-economy labs.
insights.quote: We're proposing to stop recognizing test labs in non-rescrocal economies on December 1st, 2028.

insights.claim: The FCC's position is that reciprocity is the price of entry into the US device market.
insights.speaker: Alice Jou (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Trade-style reciprocity is being imported into technical regulation.
insights.quote: reciprocity is the price of entry into the US device market

insights.claim: Since last December the FCC has administered a covered list naming entire categories of equipment by country of production, including foreign-produced drones, routers, power inverters and robotics, with certification bodies acting as first line of defense.
insights.speaker: Alice Jou (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Covered-list enforcement depends on trustworthy TCBs, linking the two policies.

insights.claim: Section 302 of the Communications Act gives the FCC broad authority over any device capable of radiating RF energy, and a Congressional amendment about 30 years ago gave explicit authority to set standards for private test labs and certification bodies.
insights.speaker: Alice Jou (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: The FCC has a durable legal basis for these rules, lowering litigation risk.
insights.quote: The FCC has an quiet superpower.

insights.claim: The FCC argues that if the gatekeeper is not accountable, even a good covered-list rule becomes hard to enforce, so lab integrity rules and the covered list must work together.
insights.speaker: Andy Hendrickson (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Equipment bans are only as effective as the certification layer.
insights.quote: So if the gatekeeper is not accountable, even a very good rule at the gate becomes sort of harder to enforce.

insights.claim: Switching labs imposes real costs on manufacturers, especially small ones, but testing is a one-time product-development expense rather than a per-unit cost, and flawed cheap reports can trigger retests and launch delays that erase savings.
insights.speaker: Andy Hendrickson (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Unit-economics impact of the rule on device makers should be modest.
insights.quote: the cheapest test isn't always the lowest cost outcome

insights.claim: The hardest constraint on reshoring testing capacity is human capital rather than equipment, since engineers who can interpret measurements take longer to develop than instruments take to buy.
insights.speaker: Andy Hendrickson (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Capacity in US and reciprocal-economy labs may be tight, benefiting incumbent testing firms with trained staff.
insights.quote: You can purchase a spectrum analyzer faster than you can develop an engineer

insights.claim: The FCC's goal is not to move all testing to the US but to build a geographically diverse network of reciprocal partners and reduce dangerous concentration.
insights.speaker: Andy Hendrickson (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Labs in allied reciprocal economies are also beneficiaries, not just US labs.

insights.claim: The FCC plans to modernize oversight with automated data tools, such as flagging unrelated products submitted with suspiciously identical measurements, under a 'verify, watch, modernize' agenda including post-market surveillance.
insights.speaker: Andy Hendrickson (FCC OET)
insights.so_what: Expect more data-driven detection of fraudulent test reports.
